passage: For months after the bullying at his school in Hanoi, Bao went straight home each day. With the school counsellor he began weekly talks. On Wednesdays the counsellor helped him name what had happened and reminded him none of it was his fault. He joined a climbing club, where Lucia, a girl from the year above, taught him to belay, and where being scared and doing it anyway felt normal. By spring he had three friends he ate lunch with. A year later the counsellor asked if Bao would talk to the Year 7s. Bao stood in front of them for ten minutes. "If someone keeps making you feel small, tell one adult early," he said. "Don't wait like I did." A boy at the back nodded.

qa.q: Who taught Bao to belay at the climbing club?
qa.a: Lucia, a girl from the year above, taught Bao to belay.

qa.q: How did Bao feel at the climbing club, and what does it show?
qa.a: Bao felt more capable and less alone there, since being scared and doing it anyway began to feel normal.

qa.q: What else could Bao do to keep helping younger students, and why?
qa.a: Bao could offer to be a lunchtime buddy for Year 7s who feel left out, because early company and a trusted person make speaking up easier.

qa.q: How might the boy at the back of the room have felt?
qa.a: The boy probably felt understood and encouraged, since someone older spoke openly about waiting too long.

grounding: With help from a counsellor, sport and a small circle of supportive friends, the student regains confidence, and later helps younger students recognise bullying and speak up early.
